data.title: Binance gets preliminary approval to establish Asia hub in Bhutan
data.description:
[BENGALURU] Binance said on Friday (Nov 27) it received in-principle approval from Bhutan’s Gelephu Central Bank to establish regulated digital-asset operations in the Himalayan kingdom, as part of its plans to expand into five Asian markets next year.

“The in-principle approval is a first step, not a full licence and Binance must satisfy the conditions specified by Gelephu Central Bank... before the relevant regulated activities may commence,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in a statement.

Binance’s expansion push follows a security breach US authorities have linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion being stolen from its platform last month and stopped all users from making withdrawals for the next two days. The company said earlier this week it has finished work to recover its withdrawal systems.

This month, SB Seker, head of Binance’s Asia-Pacific unit, told Reuters: “We have ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets... three of which are in quite mature stages.”

Seker did not specify the new markets that Binance was looking at. Binance has operating licences in 15 markets, and Seker said South and South-east Asia were key priorities.

The partnership in Bhutan will include an operational presence, with local hiring and investment in digital assets, the Binance statement on Friday said.

“Establishing an Asia hub in Gelephu Mindfulness City is a strategic decision that reflects Binance’s commitment to operating within clear, progressive regulatory frameworks,” Seker said in the statement.

Binance said it could cover the losses linked to the October cyberattack without raising fresh funds. REUTERS

data.title: Burnham’s Europe plan still taking shape as Brexit rivals circle
data.description:
[LONDON] Britain could not rejoin the European Union without another referendum, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said this week – much to the surprise of his own ministers and government officials.

While high-level discussions about Europe had taken place, and many senior figures agreed that a referendum would be inevitable in the circumstances, people familiar with the matter said they were not under the impression a final decision had been made until the PM announced it in the House of Commons.

This apparent blind siding of Burnham’s cabinet points to lack of a comprehensive strategy over Europe, critics said, just as the ruling Labour Party comes under attack from a remobilised and reinvigorated pro-Brexit movement.

Veterans of the 2016 Vote Leave campaign have recently launched new pressure groups called Stay Out and Keep Britain Out, while Burnham’s EU summit gave Nigel Farage the chance to return to Brussels and accuse the PM of betraying the referendum of a decade ago.

To be sure, Burnham has not yet taken a hit from his public flirtation with Europe. Opinion polls showed diminishing support for Brexit and Downing Street officials point to internal data suggesting almost three-quarters of voters would back a closer relationship with the bloc if it was good for the economy.

“Public negativity towards Brexit does appear strong at the moment, and therefore it is understandable on a surface why reopening elements of the Brexit debate appears low risk,” said Chris Hopkins, political director at polling firm Savanta.

“But public opinion is also fickle and there is a very real danger that raising the prominence of it could reignite the strength of feeling that led to the Brexit vote, rather than continuing on the current path.”

Since replacing Keir Starmer in July, Burnham has kept an open mind about Brexit and for now is content to pursue closer trade ties. While appearing pragmatic, there is disappointment among some Labour MPs at a lack of clear direction from the government and failure to mobilise an effective “rejoin” movement.

Without a clear decision about what comes next, they fear, the PM risks starting an almighty political fight before he has mobilised an army.

Burnham “has left the way open for the ‘Leave’ side or ‘Remain Out’ side to get very organised”, said Anand Menon, director of the UK in a Changing Europe think tank. “There’s no real leadership from Downing Street on the other side, so there’s a bit of a vacuum.”

Menon added that Labour was also opening itself up for attacks from explicitly pro-EU parties. “If the manifesto says something wishy-washy-like ‘we will continue to remove trade barriers with the EU’, I think all those progressive parties, whether it’s the SNP or Plaid or the Greens or the Lib Dems, will hammer them for being all talk and no trousers.”

The situation is complicated by the lack of a single view among senior figures and ministers as to how Burnham should proceed. Some believe rejoining is the only viable option and are frustrated at the lack of campaign mobilisation. Others are optimistic that the EU would be open to a bespoke deal with the UK to suit its needs.

In Burnham’s team, there are also those – including current and former ministers – who believe the UK should continue on its path of becoming incrementally closer to the EU through a series of deals. Those shying away from a push for full rejoin are uneasy about handing the Conservatives and Farage’s Reform UK party an easy route back.

The silver lining for Burnham may come in the form of similar splits among the pro-Brexit right.

Burnham has “chucked a grenade into the Tory Party,” said Tim Bale, professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, arguing that the bigger challenge still lies with Reform and the Tories, rather than Labour.

The issue has drawn out Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch and forced her to defend the existing Brexit deal negotiated by the Tories when in power.

“Clearly, Badenoch’s not happy talking about this,” Bale added, “and a bunch of former incredibly unsuccessful and unpopular Tory prime ministers coming out against it isn’t going to be a problem for him either.”

Two people close to Reform said Burnham’s talk of rejoining the EU was a win for them, and Farage had been reinvigorated on a return to his familiar campaigning territory, after months of scrutiny over his party’s finances.

But any hopes of a coordinated anti-EU campaign faded when Arron Banks, a long-time Brexiteer and ally of Farage, attacked the Tories and the Stay Out group when launching Keep Britain Out on Wednesday.

“Farage is making a mistake if he thinks getting the band back together and banging on about the EU is going to rescue him from the sticky situation he’s fallen into,” Bale said.

“I just don’t think it’s got the traction with the public that it had before. The problem is it puts him on the side of the status quo, rather than on the side of the insurgency.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson Holdings, Hongkong Land, Marco Polo Marine
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 27):

Jardine Matheson Holdings (JMH) , Hongkong Land : JMH announced on Thursday that Adam Keswick – whose family controls the Jardine group – will step down from the board effective Dec 31, 2026. He will also step down from the board of Hongkong Land. JMH ended Thursday at US$60.38, up US$0.25 or 0.4 per cent, while Hongkong Land was US$0.07 or 0.8 per cent higher at US$8.53, before the announcement.

Marco Polo Marine : The marine logistics company posted on Friday a 56 per cent drop in net profit to S$21.3 million for its second half ended Sep 30, 2026, from S$47.9 million in the previous corresponding period. Revenue for H2 rose 11 per cent to S$78 million from S$70.1 million. Earnings per share stood at S$0.0055 for the half-year period, down from S$0.0128. Shares of Marco Polo Marine ended at S$0.093 on Thursday, S$0.005 or 5.7 per cent higher.

data.title: China's premium puffer jacket push meets consumer resistance
data.description:
[BEIJING] Chinese shoppers are snapping up budget down jackets as the cold weather arrives, with products priced below 500 yuan (US$69) selling briskly as consumers question the value of premium brands.

A 399-yuan down jacket filled with 90 per cent goose down and produced for Peking University sold out online in mid-November after attracting widespread attention on Chinese social media. At Walmart-owned Sam’s Club, a women’s down jacket from US brand Rokka&Rolla priced at 499.9 yuan also sold out, the retailer’s app showed.

The trend marks a shift towards more cost-conscious spending in a market where people have long been pushed to buy more luxurious and expensive clothing.

Research firm iiMedia said the average price of a down jacket in China more than doubled over the past decade and was forecast to exceed 1,000 yuan in 2025. Yet a survey released this month found jackets priced between 401 yuan and 600 yuan were the most popular among consumers.

Bosideng, China’s largest down-jacket maker, has said the average price of its core products has risen to about 1,500 to 2,500 yuan.

A prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and concerns over job security have made many middle-class consumers more cautious about discretionary spending, raising questions about how much extra they are willing to pay for premium outerwear.

“I think Sam’s has nailed that with its down jackets,” said Mark Tanner, founder and managing director of Shanghai-based consultancy China Skinny.

“Many shoppers are not hunting for the cheapest copy. They want comparable design, function or pleasure without paying a large prestige premium,” he said.

The challenge is becoming increasingly apparent for brands seeking to move further upmarket. Bosideng this month launched its third collection from British designer Kim Jones, but some higher-priced items saw limited sales on its flagship store on Tmall, an upmarket online shopping platform.

A blue jacket featured in advertisements with singer, actor and brand ambassador Wang Leehom carried a price tag of about 2,278 yuan but sold just 16 units in the 30 days to Nov 13, according to figures displayed on the Tmall store.

Bosideng did not respond to a request for comment.

Value over prestige

The diverging fortunes suggest consumers are becoming more selective rather than simply trading down.

More than 30 million down jackets were sold during this year’s Singles’ Day shopping festival, according to e-commerce giant Alibaba, while Uniqlo and Bosideng ranked first and second by sales, retaining their long-held positions at the top of China’s down-jacket market.

Uniqlo surpassed 100 million yuan in Tmall sales within 24 minutes of Singles’ Day promotions launching on Oct 20, Tmall said, and the platform listed the brand’s lightweight down jacket, which typically retails for around 500 yuan in China, among its top-selling products.

Demand also remains resilient at the top end. Canada Goose said Greater China revenue rose 32.5 per cent in the quarter ended September.

“China is a very healthy region for Moncler,” chief corporate and supply officer Luciano Santel said last month, as the premium outerwear brand continued to outperform a broader luxury slowdown in the world’s second-largest economy.

“Like every luxury brand, they’ll need to work harder than ever to justify the premium price point,” Tanner said.

The contrasting performances reflect a broader divergence in Chinese consumption. As economic uncertainty weighs on middle-class households, many consumers are trading down or demanding greater value for money, while wealthier shoppers continue spending on products they believe offer them quality, performance or status.

“I definitely won’t buy another down jacket that costs more than 1,000 yuan,” said Lv Jiaming, a 27-year-old factory worker in Shanghai. “To me, there isn’t much difference between a jacket priced at 500 or 600 yuan and one that costs more than 1,000 yuan. You can’t really feel the difference, unless it’s exceptionally good.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Kimly, AP Oil, Heptamax
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 26):

Kimly : The coffee shop operator reported a 30.8 per cent fall in net profit to S$12.8 million for its second half ended Sep 30, from S$18.5 million a year earlier. Revenue came in 1 per cent lower at S$161.1 million, from S$162.8 million previously. Kimly proposed a final dividend of S$0.01 a share for H2, bringing the total FY2026 dividend to S$0.02 a share. Shares of Kimly ended flat at S$0.365 on Wednesday, before the news.

AP Oil : The CEO of the petroleum products company, Ho Chee Hon, was sentenced to six months jail and a fine of S$25,000 for drink-driving on Wednesday. Accordingly, he will be away on a leave of absence for a period of six months from Dec 1. The company said that the charges are personal in nature and unrelated to its business or operations. Its board added that Ho remains suitable to continue in his role as CEO. Shares of AP Oil ended flat at S$0.126 on Wednesday, before the update.

Heptamax : The industrial solutions company, which is proposing to buy a data centre company for S$500 million in a reverse takeover, has been queried by the Singapore Exchange Regulation over the deal. Among other things, the regulator asked how the valuation for the target company Racks Central was arrived at. It also asked Heptamax to give details of the beneficial owners of the vendor. The company replied that the price was arrived at on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis, taking into account Racks Central’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for FY2025, among other things. Heptamax ended flat at S$0.131 on Wednesday.

data.title: Banks facing bond price-fixing trial agree to pay over US$400 million
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Wall Street firms, including some of the industry’s biggest banks, are on track to pay more than US$400 million to end a high-stakes lawsuit claiming they schemed to fix prices in the muni bond market.

The deal would end a long-running federal class-action suit that reached the doorstep of the US Supreme Court and was heading to a jury trial, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

The proposed payment – a fraction of the billions that plaintiffs demanded – was hashed out in recent days and may be presented to a court soon, one of the people said, asking not to be identified discussing the confidential talks. 

Municipalities led by Philadelphia had accused a group of banks including JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs of colluding to set interest rates artificially high on a certain kind of debt, positioning the firms to profit at the expense of taxpayers. 

The firms have disputed the allegations in court. Representatives for the cities and those banks declined to comment on any settlement talks. Morgan Stanley said in a quarterly regulatory filing that the parties had reached a settlement in principle, without disclosing the amount.

The municipalities were also suing units of Citigroup, Bank of America, Barclays, Royal Bank of Canada and Wells Fargo. Representatives for those banks either declined to comment or didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

A public trial threatened to place another harsh spotlight on Wall Street’s treatment of Main Street, bringing with it risks of reputational damage on top of financial demands that swelled during litigation. Documents filed to the Supreme Court showed municipalities hoped to ultimately win US$12 billion.

The allegations centred on so-called variable-rate demand obligations. The long-term bonds, dubbed VRDOs, have their rates periodically reset and offer investors the opportunity to return the securities for cash if they think the yields are reset too low. 

The municipalities accused the banks of conspiring to inflate those rates above competitive levels to increase the chances of placing the VRDOs with an investor rather than having to keep them in their own inventory. 

The claims followed findings of manipulation in the global foreign-exchange market and in setting Libor, the London interbank offered rate. Those scandals cost dozens of traders their jobs and banks billions in fines and penalties.

In their Supreme Court appeal, the banks said municipalities hadn’t met one of the class-action requirements by showing that issues common to all of the plaintiffs would predominate over individual questions. The banks hoped to overturn a federal appeals court decision that let the class action go forward.

The banks are separately defending against related claims in state court in New York and California under the US False Claims Act. Bloomberg Intelligence analysts estimated in July that settling the antitrust action would likely cost banks about US$770 million along with an additional few hundred million dollars to resolve state court actions.

Though the allegations focused on an esoteric corner of a complex market, lawyers for the municipalities would have set out to make a more straightforward argument in a trial: That banks made promises to clients and didn’t live up to them. BLOOMBERG

data.title: The portfolio career is not what most people think
data.description:
FOR most of my career, the question “What do you do?” had a fairly straightforward answer. Today, it runs a little longer.

I teach. I consult. I run a merchandise business. I write, and I am working on a book.

At first glance, that looks fragmented. Yet the value lies precisely in the overlap. Consulting gives me real business problems to bring into the classroom. Teaching forces me to explain ideas more clearly.

Writing makes me think harder about what I actually believe. Running a business ensures whatever I say about strategy will actually survive customers, costs and cash flow.

My “portfolio career” is not simply about doing several things but designing them so that each makes the others more valuable.

Start with a core, then build around it

Portfolio careers are often discussed in terms of flexibility or multiple income streams. Those benefits matter, but they undersell the model.

Most successful portfolios need a central piece – an expertise, profession or capability developed deeply enough that other activities can grow around it.

This is why I do not see a portfolio career as a rejection of a conventional one. Years spent inside organisations build expertise, credibility, networks and pattern recognition that can later be deployed in different settings.

What looks like diversification later in life is often built on considerable concentration earlier.

For someone considering this pathway, the first move need not involve resigning. Guest lecturing once a semester, joining a non-profit or industry board, advising a startup, mentoring, writing regularly or taking on a fractional role can all extend existing expertise into new contexts.

You are not starting over. You are finding more ways to use what you have spent years learning.

A portfolio career is also a strategy challenge

In teaching, I often say a good strategy does not just rely on existing strengths; making different choices reinforce one another creates new strength.

A consulting assignment may produce an idea for a lesson. A classroom discussion may sharpen an argument for an article. Writing forces me to structure that argument more rigorously, while running a business provides real-life material that eventually finds its way back into teaching and writing.

The same principle applies when deciding what to add to the portfolio.

Increasingly, I ask three questions: Do I like doing it? Am I good at it? And does it pay well?

“Pay” here is broader than money.

A non-profit board role may offer purpose, governance experience and relationships. Teaching may not compete with a corporate salary, but it sharpens communication and exposes you to younger perspectives.

Writing a book may take years before producing meaningful income, yet it could deepen expertise and open doors elsewhere.

Few activities score perfectly on all three dimensions. A portfolio gives you more room because different roles can provide different returns.

“Less package tour, more independent travel”

Brandon Lee, chief futures at the Skills & Workforce Development Agency and a strong advocate of independent work, has described the future of work as becoming more deconstructed: “Less package tour, more independent travel.”

I like that analogy.

Traditionally, an employer bundled salary, identity, colleagues, training and progression together. Increasingly, experienced professionals can assemble more of those components themselves through different forms of work.

Artificial intelligence lowers the threshold further. Research, writing, analysis and other capabilities that once required substantial organisational infrastructure can increasingly be handled by individuals or small teams.

Yet portfolio work makes something else more obvious: relationships matter.

Knowing how to do good work is necessary, but opportunities often come through people who know, trust and are prepared to recommend you.

AI makes expertise easier to deploy independently, but relationships often determine where that expertise gets deployed.

Meanwhile, the system needs to recognise less conventional forms of work as legitimate contributions. This matters because portfolio careers become much easier to build when employers stop treating every departure from a full-time job as an awkward gap that needs explaining.

Using the optionality you have built

Author and LinkedIn opinion leader Eric Sim, who has 2.8 million followers on the platform, has described the window in life when one has money, time and health at the same time as the “magical stage”.

After a career in banking, Sim now writes, speaks professionally, coaches, and teaches finance.

A portfolio career provides one way to extend the duration of this window. Instead of postponing different interests until retirement, accumulated experience and financial security allow work to be assembled differently.

My own philosophy has become simpler with age: do things I like, or do things with people I like. Even better if I can do things I like with people I like.

A portfolio career allows those different motivations to coexist instead of forcing one job to satisfy all of them.

The real payoff from years spent building “career capital” may not be another title, but greater control over what you do, with whom and why.

Know what not to add

There is, of course, a danger of romanticising all this. Every new commitment consumes attention, often a scarcer resource than time. Four unrelated gigs can simply mean four sets of deadlines.

The harder part may then be deciding what does not belong.

Does a new role deepen something you already do? Does it bring you into contact with people you genuinely want to work with? Does it create knowledge, experience or opportunities that can travel across the rest of your portfolio?

Your answers should guide you.

For much of our careers, success was defined by how far we climbed one ladder. A portfolio career offers a different vantage point.

Like good strategy, the strength of that portfolio will come from how well your choices fit together.

The writer is a former economist who now wears several professional hats. Between guest lecturing and running businesses, he is co-authoring a forthcoming book, The China Mindset.

data.title: US shoppers confront uphill battle in Black Friday discount quest
data.description:
[LOS ANGELES] Inflation-weary US shoppers thronged malls and websites on Black Friday, the traditional kick-off to the holiday spending season, but many said they were struggling to find robust enough bargains to counter the pinch of high gas and grocery prices.

Spending is seen topping last year’s strong results by 4 to 6 per cent, and early Black Friday figures point to particularly robust online growth. But brick-and-mortar foot traffic was mixed, and beneath top-line forecasts lie signs of stress.

Most of the gains will be attributable to inflation – which at 3.8 per cent is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years – while consumer sentiment remains shaky.

Jasmine Peters, 37, went to the Westfield Century City mall in Los Angeles on Friday hoping to find steeper discounts in-store than online, but they didn’t materialise, and by late morning, she was planning to leave the mall empty-handed.

Chris Nile, 30, was hoping for more than the US$50 discount he saw on a Nintendo Switch 2 gaming console, which brought the price to US$450. “Inflation is higher – hell, even the (McDonald’s) McChicken is up,” said Nile as he shopped for his two boys at the Crabtree Valley Mall in Raleigh, North Carolina.

Observers said consumers seemed less impressed by discounts, with stores needing to do more to draw them in. Target, for example, gave away US$100 gift cards to the first 100 people in line at each store – with one lucky recipient receiving a US$1,000 card.

“Traffic levels in general seemed off compared to past holidays and seemed to lose steam early,” said Michael Brown, Americas retail leader at consulting firm Kearney, who visited several stores in Westchester County, New York, on Friday morning.

US store visits were tracking 2.4 per cent behind last year’s, at 760 million a little after 6.30 pm EST, according to Passby, a geospatial analytics company that measures real-time foot traffic.

A November survey by the National Retail Federation found that 82 per cent of consumers are taking steps to manage holiday costs this year, like buying less expensive gifts. Nile – like many US shoppers – said he chose to bargain-hunt in person, in part to avoid shipping costs.

Artificial intelligence could also scramble the year’s shopping dynamics. As consumers use it to find bargains or even complete purchases – and retailers become increasingly adept at altering prices – the deepest discounts could come closer to Christmas.

Online spending on Black Friday itself, though, jumped 12.8 per cent from a year ago to US$9.7 billion, according to initial figures through 6.30 pm EST from Adobe Analytics, the arm of Adobe that analyses customer behaviour. That figure put the day on track to surpass Adobe’s prediction for a 9.2 per cent increase.

The first half of the day alone drove US$5.9 billion in US online sales, up 2.9 per cent from a year ago, Salesforce data showed.

Measured growth

Economic worries aside, top-line spending is expected to be robust.

Thanksgiving Day saw consumers spend US$7.1 billion online, according to Adobe, a 10.4 per cent jump over last year, fuelled by big discounts on electronics, toys and apparel.

Indeed, store visits to electronics retailer Best Buy were tracking 3.2 per cent higher than last Black Friday in the late afternoon, according to Passby. Visits to Walmart and Target were slightly up.

Overall, the National Retail Federation sees November to December holiday retail sales rising 4.2 per cent year over year, to just above US$1 trillion.

High living costs emerged as a key issue earlier this month when voters handed Democrats sweeping electoral victories, punishing US President Donald Trump for an Iran war that’s pushed the cost of living higher.

Even higher earners may be stretched.

Holiday spending forecasts mostly predated the recent stock market correction that followed the midterms, turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, and mounting concerns around an AI bubble. The decline could dampen the wealth effect that has seen affluent shoppers splurge, UBS analysts said in a note on Tuesday.

Embattled toys

Higher input costs, particularly from oil derivatives like plastic, are hitting some products more than others.

Prices of toys – generally high in plastic – have risen 13.2 per cent since the start of the year, pushing Barbie maker Mattel this month to cut its annual forecast as consumers balked at higher costs.

But some unlikely products are buoying the toy category. Best Buy and Target have both flagged trading cards – including Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering products – as a key growth driver. Squishy NeeDoh toys are also in hot demand, according to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend.

Lego also appeared to be in high demand, with the Passby figures showing its stores’ foot traffic up more than 5 per cent in mid-afternoon versus the same time of day last Black Friday. It was not necessarily kids driving the growth – many of those shopping were adults, part of the “kidult” craze that has swept the toy industry in recent years.

Jaime Oquendo, 46, was the first to enter the Lego store at the Westfield Century City mall in Los Angeles when it opened, to buy a new Godzilla set, released on Black Friday at US$450.

“I actually made sure I had money set aside all year, back when they announced it, just to make sure I could get my hands on one,” Oquendo said. REUTERS

data.title: Why COP31 is not a total failure
data.description:
THE collapse of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, has sent shockwaves across much of the globe, marking the first time in 17 years that a UN Climate Conference ended without a consensus agreement.

It might even come to be seen as a wake-up call to the world to get more serious about tackling global warming.

However, the event was not a total failure.

One indicator of progress is the Global Climate Action Agenda Electrification Delivery Package. According to the United Nations, more than 260 businesses, with over US$4 trillion in combined annual revenue, announced or profiled actions related to this initiative at COP31.

This also underlines how the centre of gravity at recent COPs has shifted from the negotiating zone of government officials – important as they remain – to a wider ecosystem of investors, technology experts, business leaders, scientists and civil society groups.

COPs have evolved from medium-sized policymaking gatherings into massive events encompassing wider corporate trade fairs and roadshows with growing industry participation, including from the Asia-Pacific.

COP21 in 2015 in Paris, where the landmark global climate deal was agreed, drew around 25,000 attendees. By contrast, Antalya gathered nearly quadruple that overall attendance, making it the largest climate summit ever.

The Electrification Delivery Package itself involved major multinational corporations including Mahindra, Octopus Energy, Unilever, Siemens, Iberdrola, Schneider Electric, Volvo Cars, Fortescue, Nestle, Orsted and SSE.

It is not just the private sector getting behind this electrification push. Some 150 countries plus the European Union, accounting for more than two-thirds of world gross domestic product, have also signed up.

From the C40 Cities group – a global coalition of urban centres seeking to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and meet wider environmental objectives – 37 member cities agreed to either report electrification progress in 2026 or announce actions for 2027.

Beyond this specific package, which will result in billions of dollars in clean energy investment, is a wider 35x35 Electrification Pledge. The voluntary pledge aims to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, from just over 20 per cent today.

The pledge, backed by countries representing around half of the global economy according to the UN, has also been championed by the International Energy Agency, which asserted that “the world has entered the Age of Electricity”.

While the proposed Antalya Pact was not agreed at COP31, the electrification deals send market signals on where the global energy system is heading – just as early renewable power investment did in the past.

With a vanguard of companies already pushing forward, a global benchmark has been established for the future electric economy around which private capital can mobilise.

COP reform still needed

While the COPs remain important events where the private sector can play a constructive role, reform is needed to maximise the momentum coming out of them.

Anything less will threaten the legitimacy of future summits, including COP32 in Africa in 2027, which will now require supreme political skill to deliver.

At the heart of change is the need to adapt the consensus rule. This currently allows a very small number of states and their allies to exercise an effective veto and curtail global climate ambition.

One of the sharpest criticisms of COP31, voiced by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and key powers such as the EU, is the blocking role played by oil states. It highlights how geopolitical divisions, from the Ukraine war to the Iran crisis, are making COP diplomacy far harder to navigate.

Such diplomatic gridlock creates uncertainty for mobilising private capital. To be sure, the private sector can see broad changes in direction of travel. But the clarity and strength of policy signals still determine the speed and extent to which companies react.

This matters all the more because the next few years of global climate diplomacy will largely determine whether the 2015 Paris Agreement succeeds or fails.

Major economies are still working to deliver on their latest Nationally Determined Contributions – country-level emission reduction targets under the Paris Agreement – where the private sector has a huge role to play.

Nations must not only put forward greater ambition, but also follow through on it if the world is going to get anywhere near the Paris goals.

Amid this uncertainty, the danger for future COPs is that summits settle for a lowest-common-denominator outcome, even if total collapse is avoided. The world needs much more.

That is why there is growing urgency to reform how global climate diplomacy works. COP31 was not an outright failure, as the electrification initiatives show, but without fixing the negotiating process, policymakers risk slowing down the very capital ready to fund the transition.

The writer is an associate at LSE IDEAS at the London School of Economics

While the COPs remain important events where the private sector can play a constructive role, reform is needed to maximise the momentum coming out of them.

Anything less will threaten the legitimacy of future summits, including COP32 in Africa in 2027, which will now require supreme political skill to deliver.

At the heart of change is the need to adapt the consensus rule. This currently allows a very small number of states and their allies to exercise an effective veto and curtail global climate ambition.

One of the sharpest criticisms of COP31, voiced by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and key powers such as the EU, is the blocking role played by oil states. It highlights how geopolitical divisions, from the Ukraine war to the Iran crisis, are making COP diplomacy far harder to navigate.

Such diplomatic gridlock creates uncertainty for mobilising private capital. To be sure, the private sector can see broad changes in direction of travel. But the clarity and strength of policy signals still determine the speed and extent to which companies react.

This matters all the more because the next few years of global climate diplomacy will largely determine whether the 2015 Paris Agreement succeeds or fails.

Major economies are still working to deliver on their latest Nationally Determined Contributions – country-level emission reduction targets under the Paris Agreement – where the private sector has a huge role to play.

Nations must not only put forward greater ambition, but also follow through on it if the world is going to get anywhere near the Paris goals.

Amid this uncertainty, the danger for future COPs is that summits settle for a lowest-common-denominator outcome, even if total collapse is avoided. The world needs much more.

That is why there is growing urgency to reform how global climate diplomacy works. COP31 was not an outright failure, as the electrification initiatives show, but without fixing the negotiating process, policymakers risk slowing down the very capital ready to fund the transition.

The writer is an associate at LSE IDEAS at the London School of Economics
